ExplanationParts.CorpusEarnedOpening: Thirty years later is ordinary future time turned into a recurring public reckoning: the Chan records use it to forecast how a saying, encounter, or person will be laughed at, understood, repeated, or misreported.
EvidenceBody: Yuanwu Keqin warns his assembly not to repeat his holding-fast and letting-go question wrongly thirty years later; elsewhere he postpones an answer until this mountain monk has changed his bones. When a monk predicts that people will laugh in thirty years, Dahui Zonggao immediately asks why wait and says people already laugh. Nanyang Huizhong predicts that a genuine monk will be hard to find, Guishan Lingyou says an encounter will later ring when struck, and Kaixian Shanxian says future people will know. Chengxin Shengzong's warning not to fail him later keeps the expression a forecast and test, not an instruction to wait a prescribed interval.

DraftEvidence.ZenBend: A plain future date repeatedly caps present encounters by deferring their public recognition, laughter, repetition, or correction.
DraftEvidence.CounterexampleOrLimit: The words also occur as ordinary chronology, and Dahui challenges the delay itself; the phrase does not lexically mean verdict or prescribe a waiting period.

that future point used as a deferred public reckoning
